m202.text: A magnet, a steel pin and a copper wire! The pin and the wire are both metal. Which one will the magnet pull?

m203.text: One, the steel pin. Two, the copper wire. Three, both.

m301.text: Today, a brand-new theme begins, and it starts with magnets!

m302.text: A little pigeon is hiding in this video. Can you spot it?

m303b.text: Pigeons love our void deck. Look up high, on the ledges and the pipes!

m304.text: You against the Buddies! Lock in first with your fingers. One finger for every point.

h501.text: Are you ready? Three! Two! One! Go!

m501.text: Round one! Which one will the magnet pull? Show me your fingers!

m503m.text: One! In Grandma's sewing box, a magnet picks up the steel pins. I have seen it!

m504p.text: Two. The copper wire is thinner and lighter, so it should be easier to pull.

m505b.text: Three, both! They are both metal, and my magnet pulls metal. Easy!

m601m.text: Basil, your magnet is smooth and painted, like a toy. Is it made of plastic?

m602.text: Look closer. Long ago, people found a special kind of rock that pulls on iron.

m603.text: A natural magnet is also called a lodestone.

m604p.text: A lodestone is a magnet that comes from the ground. Nobody made it!

m605.text: Now look inside Basil's magnet. Under the paint, it is made of metal, usually iron or steel.

m607b.text: And magnets come in lots of shapes: bar, U-shaped, button, rod, ring and horseshoe!

m609.text: A magnet is an object that is usually made of iron or steel.

m701.text: Be a steel pin! Shrink down. Quietly.

m702.text: You are a steel pin, lying on the test table. Beside you, the copper wire looks like a big orange pipe.

m703.text: Here comes the magnet, like a giant red and blue tower. It is still far away, so nothing happens.

m704.text: Closer, and closer. You feel a tug. Then whoosh! You slide across the gap, and click onto the magnet.

m705.text: The magnet lifts you up. Look down. The copper wire and the eraser have not moved at all.

m801.text: The answer is one: the steel pin! Did you show one finger? Put one finger up!

m802m.text: The magnet pulled the steel pin across the gap. But the copper wire did not move at all!

m803.text: Pip, the copper wire is very light, but the magnet still did not pull it. So being light is not the reason.

m901m.text: My turn! I tested Mum's iron wok. The magnet could not lift it, so the wok is not attracted to the magnet!

m902.text: Something is not right. If you can spot it, cross your arms. Hold on!

m904p.text: Watch. When I let go, the magnet holds on to the side of the wok. The wok is attracted. It is just too heavy to lift!

m905.text: A fridge magnet cannot lift your fridge either, but it holds on to the fridge door.

m1001b.text: So my magnet sticks to the wok, like glue! Is my magnet sticky?

m1002.text: Look closer, in slow motion. The pin starts to move before it touches the magnet. It jumps across the gap.

m1004.text: The magnet pulls the pin towards it. We say the magnet attracts the pin.

m1005b.text: Attract means pull! My magnet pulls the pin, even before they touch. So it is not sticky at all!

m1006.text: The pin is made of steel, and the nail is made of iron. They are made of magnetic materials.

m1007p.text: Magnetic materials are the materials that a magnet attracts. Iron and steel are magnetic materials!

m1009.text: Magnets attract objects made of magnetic materials. Magnetic materials include iron and steel.

m1101.text: Show me your score hand! One finger or more? You beat the Buddies. Two fingers? High five!

m1102.text: Did you spot the pigeon? It was on top of the bicycle rack!

m1103m.text: Here is a fun fact! Scientists think pigeons can sense the Earth's magnetism. It helps them find their way home, even from far away!

h860.text: Let's read today's key words together! Ready?

m1201b.text: Wait! Copper is a metal, just like iron and steel. So why does my magnet ignore the copper wire?
